subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In a four-figure grid reference, which coordinate is read first?
questions.explain: Grid references are read 'along the corridor and up the stairs', so eastings (the horizontal value) are always given before northings.

questions.q: A six-figure grid reference locates a point to the nearest:
questions.explain: A six-figure reference divides each one-kilometre grid square into tenths, pinpointing a location to within 100 metres.

questions.q: On a map with a scale of 1:50 000, one centimetre on the map represents:
questions.explain: At 1:50 000, 1 cm represents 50 000 cm, which equals 500 metres on the ground.

questions.q: Contour lines on an Ordnance Survey map join points of equal:
questions.explain: Contour lines are isolines that connect points of the same height above sea level, showing relief.

questions.q: Contour lines drawn very close together on a map indicate:
questions.explain: The closer together the contour lines, the greater the change in height over a short distance, indicating a steep gradient.

questions.q: What is the compass bearing of a place due west of an observer?
questions.explain: Bearings are measured clockwise from north (000°), so due west is three-quarters of the way round at 270°.

questions.q: Two features are 6 cm apart on a map with a scale of 1:25 000. What is the actual distance between them?
questions.explain: At 1:25 000, 1 cm represents 250 m, so 6 cm represents 1500 m, which is 1.5 km.

questions.q: On a climate graph, precipitation (rainfall) is usually shown using:
questions.explain: By convention, a climate graph shows monthly rainfall as bars and temperature as a line.

questions.q: A population pyramid is used to display:
options: The age and sex structure of a population
The average temperature of a place
The proportions that make up a total
questions.explain: A population pyramid is a back-to-back bar graph showing the percentage of males and females in each age group.

questions.q: The mean of a set of values is found by:
options: Adding all the values and dividing by the number of values
Selecting the middle value when placed in order
Subtracting the smallest value from the largest
questions.explain: The mean is the arithmetic average, calculated as the sum of all values divided by how many values there are.

questions.q: The median of a data set is:
options: The middle value when the data are arranged in order
The average of all the values
The difference between the highest and lowest value
questions.explain: The median is the central value of an ordered data set, with an equal number of values above and below it.

questions.q: A scatter graph is most useful for showing:
options: Change in a single value over time only
The proportions of different categories in a whole
The age structure of a population
questions.explain: A scatter graph plots pairs of values to reveal any correlation between two variables.

questions.q: For the data set 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, what is the mode?
questions.explain: The mode is the value that appears most often, and 7 occurs twice while all others occur once.

questions.q: On a pie chart, a category that represents 25% of the total would occupy an angle of:
questions.explain: A full pie chart is 360°, and 25% of 360° is 90°.

questions.q: Data collected first-hand by a student during fieldwork is known as:
questions.explain: Primary data is original information gathered directly in the field, such as traffic counts or river measurements.

questions.q: Secondary data is best described as information that is:
options: Obtained from published sources such as census records
questions.explain: Secondary data has been collected and published by someone else, for example census statistics, maps or textbooks.

questions.q: In systematic sampling, data points are selected:
options: At regular intervals, such as every tenth house
Wherever is most convenient for the researcher
questions.explain: Systematic sampling collects data at fixed, regular intervals to give an even coverage of the study area.

questions.q: In random sampling, every item in the study area has:
options: An equal chance of being selected
Selection based on the researcher's judgement
Selection in proportion to its group size
questions.explain: Random sampling gives every location or item the same probability of selection, reducing bias.

questions.q: In a river fieldwork study, discharge is calculated as:
questions.explain: Discharge, the volume of water passing a point per second, equals the channel's cross-sectional area multiplied by the water's velocity.

questions.q: Qualitative data collected in fieldwork is best described as:
options: Descriptive information about qualities or opinions
Data that can always be plotted on a bar graph
questions.explain: Qualitative data is non-numerical, describing qualities, opinions or characteristics, such as responses about how attractive an area feels.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Geography (0460) syllabus; Geographical Skills
